title: Read scatter plots and correlation
show: scatter plot of the five (x,y) points showing the trend direction

example.question:
A teacher records hours of TV watched, $x$, and test score, $y$, for five students.
$x$: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
$y$: 9, 7, 6, 3, 2
The points lie close to a straight line sloping downhill. Choose the value of $r$ from $0.99$, $-0.2$, $-0.99$ and explain your choice.

steps.say: Look at which way the points run. As $x$ goes up, $y$ goes down, so the **direction** is negative. That rules out $0.99$.
Look at how tight the points are. They lie close to one straight line, so the link is **strong**. A value near $0$, like $-0.2$, means a loose cloud.

rows.aside: Close to a line: strong, so $r$ is near $-1$

steps.say: Strong and negative means $r$ is close to $-1$. Give the value, then say it in words.

rows.aside: Strong negative linear correlation: as TV time goes up, test score goes down.

title: Recognise outliers
show: box plot with fences at Q1-1.5IQR and Q3+1.5IQR and the outlier point marked beyond

example.question:
Find any outliers in this data set, using the rule that an outlier lies more than $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ above $Q_3$ or below $Q_1$.
$3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 30$

steps.say: The data is already in order. Find $\hl{1}{Q_1}$ and $\hl{2}{Q_3}$, the medians of the lower and upper halves.
Subtract the quartiles to get the width of the middle half.
Go $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ beyond each quartile. Beyond these, a value is an outlier.
Check the smallest and largest values against the fences. Only $30$ is outside.

title: Estimate the mean of grouped data
show: histogram of minutes spent on homework with classes 0-10 to 30-40

example.question:
The table shows the number of minutes 20 students spent on homework.
Minutes: 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40
Number of students: 3, 7, 6, 4
Estimate the mean time.

steps.say: Take the middle of each group. Add the two ends and halve.
Multiply each mid-value $\hl{1}{x}$ by the number of students $f$, then add them up.
Add the frequencies to get the number of students, then divide.

title: Select an appropriate graphical/numerical summary
show: dot plot of 5,6,6,7,8,40 showing the outlier pulling the mean

example.question: Six students are asked how much pocket money they get each week (in euro): $5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 40$. Which average describes a typical student better, the mean or the median? Calculate both and give a reason.
example.final: \text{Median} = 6.5\text{, because the extreme value } 40 \text{ pulls the mean up to } 12

steps.say: Look at the data first. One value, $\hl{1}{40}$, is far bigger than the rest. An extreme value drags the mean up but hardly moves the median.

rows.aside: Five students get $8$ or less. One gets $40$.

steps.say: Add the values and divide by how many there are.
The data is already in order. With six values, the median is halfway between the 3rd and 4th.
The mean of $12$ is bigger than what five of the six students get. The median is not pulled by the $40$.

rows.aside: Use the **median**: the $40$ is extreme, so the mean is not typical.
